newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian government to review economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: Russian government to review economic reforms.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin issued a fresh flurry of decrees ahead of a meeting of his ministers to review their efforts to push through economic and social reforms.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin will chair Thursday's session in the absence of Yeltsin, who has maintained a heavy workload while vacationing at the Volzhsky Utyos resort by the river Volga in central Russia.

Yeltsin, who held talks with First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov and other leaders, signed decrees on Wednesday aimed at relieving chronic delays in payment of state salaries, clamping down on tax debtors and increasing gold exports.

Yeltsin brought Nemtsov and another reformist, First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, into the government early this year, giving them free hand to pursue economic reforms and promising to back them in the potentially painful process.

Though on holiday since early July, Yeltsin, 66, has made clear that he remains in charge, firing off a steady salvo of commands on a wide range of issues from army reform to tax dodgers while enjoying his hobbies of fishing and tennis.

Yeltsin, who underwent a quintuple heart bypass operation last November, boasted of his good health after taking Renat Akchurin, who performed the surgery, to a banya (sauna) where a bundle of birch twigs is traditionally used to invigorate blood circulation.

"In order to prove to him that my heart works like a clock, I took him to the banya," Yeltsin said. "First he worked on me with the birch twigs and then I worked on him. We found out that his pulse was quicker than mine after that."

Yeltsin earlier delighted human rights groups and outraged his communist and nationalist opponents by vetoing a controversial bill that would have imposed tough curbs on evangelical Christians, Roman Catholics and other "non-traditional" religious groups.

In a statement released by the Kremlin, he defended his veto of the draft law, "On Freedom of Conscience and Religious Association," saying it contradicted Russia's constitution guaranteeing equality for all confessions.

"Of course the state can and must limit the activity of pseudo-religious organisations that bring harm to the morality and health of the population. But this does not mean the state can trample on fundamental human rights," the statement said.

Yeltsin's veto of a bill overwhelmingly approved by both houses of parliament and strongly endorsed by the powerful Russian Orthodox Church suggested he had not lost his taste for taking risks and alienating political opponents even further.
